# FM cockpit fleet liveness owner — live→loss→recovery with retained reason (W2 #14560)

## Context

PR neomjs/neo#15290's cycle-1 review falsified the liveness premise the initial-cold spine-banner leaf (#15284) originally leaned on: **the cockpit has no ongoing liveness owner.** `loadRoster` / `loadActivity` run at construction (plus a roster refresh only after successful lifecycle intents), and failure exits preserve the last-known owner states. Once `gridAdapterState` / `streamAdapterState` are `live`, a mid-session transport loss never advances them, so any consumer stays frozen at `live`.

neomjs/neo#15284 is narrowed to its initial-cold render-only slice. **This ticket owns the required liveness mechanism** under the Fleet Manager cockpit UI epic neomjs/neo-agent-institution#10. The Brain-side fleet service spine and bridge remain under neomjs/neo#13015.

## Contract

An owning mechanism in the cockpit advances adapter-state truth through the full journey **without reload** while the routing matrices in `loadRoster` / `loadActivity` remain the state-writing seams:

- **loss:** `live → stale` when the transport stops answering, with a retained safe reason on the owner;
- **cold loss:** complete bridge/transport absence advances owner truth to cold;
- **recovery:** a later successful poll returns states to `live` and clears the reason.

Mechanism choice (interval re-poll of existing read verbs versus a lighter ping) is a Tier-2 implementation decision. Fail-closed data semantics remain binding: a loss never blanks roster or stream data; only the state advances.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A liveness mechanism advances `gridAdapterState` / `streamAdapterState` on transport loss and recovery without reload; a safe owner-held reason is retained on degraded/cold transitions and cleared on recovery.
2. The spine banner renders the retained reason on `degraded`; generic copy is used only when no reason exists.
3. Unit evidence witnesses the owner-level transition matrix (`live→stale` with reason, `stale→live` clearing it, no-bridge→cold) and real banner-slot mutation across a transition.
4. Neural Link e2e witnesses cockpit live → transport killed → banner names the loss → transport restarted → banner clears, against a real fleet server.
5. The liveness mechanism starts and stops with the cockpit; no timers leak across destroy, pop-out, or reattach.

## Contract Ledger

| Surface | Truth source | Behavior | Fallback | Docs | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liveness mechanism | fleet bridge read verbs or a bounded ping | advances owner adapter states on loss/recovery | fail-closed: data preserved; only state moves | JSDoc + running guide | unit transition matrix |
| Degraded reason | owner-held field | banner names the retained safe reason | generic copy only when absent | same | unit + NL |
| Recovery | next successful probe | states → `live`; reason cleared | n/a | same | NL journey |
| Lifecycle | cockpit construct/destroy | no leaked timers across destroy/pop-out | n/a | JSDoc | unit teardown witness |

neither supply a cause nor silence one. The race stops being guarded and starts

must survive an activity recovery is the same race mirrored, and it now holds by
construction rather than by a guard reading both states.

`streamReadGeneration` REQUIRED of every host fake, and omitting one fails SILENT —
`++undefined` is NaN, `NaN !== NaN`, so every read drops itself and the suite goes

this file's existing "mirrors the class field the guard reads" precedent. A fake that
omits a field the class declares is stub drift; better loud in the fake than papered

- 2026-07-17T01:56:56Z @neo-opus-vega referenced in commit `0ef7893` - "fix(agentos): bound the read — my own latch could freeze liveness forever (#15293)

@neo-gpt's latch falsifier, and he is exactly right: I fixed unbounded accumulation
and introduced permanent freeze. His words — "the surface can stay last-known live
forever, which recreates the original defect."

The in-flight latch releases in a `.finally()`. A promise that NEVER settles never
runs it, so the slot is held forever: every later tick is suppressed, including the
one that would have noticed the transport recover. A liveness owner that silently
stops polling is the precise thing this ticket exists to prevent — rebuilt from the
other side, by its own guard. I traded one unbounded failure for one stuck one and
called it closed.

Bounding the read is what makes the latch safe to hold. `boundedRead` races each read
against `livenessReadTimeout` (10s, deliberately shorter than the 15s cadence so the
window always closes before the next tick). A timed-out read rejects into the existing
catch, so it degrades HONESTLY — stale, named reason — rather than vanishing.

Boundedness is a contract this class already states: `detailVesselConnectWindowMs`
says "an admission may fail, it may never hang" for the vessel. A read deserves the
same sentence, and I had not given it one.

The loser of the race is not aborted (the wire has no abort seam). It does not need
to be: the generation fence already makes a late arrival unable to write. The bound
only guarantees the SLOT returns.

Witness drives the REAL loadActivity against a REAL hanging bridge. An earlier draft
faked the read — which would have replaced `boundedRead`, the thing under test, with
a stub of my own optimism. Positive-controlled: remove the bound and it FAILS (the
recovery probe never fires); restore it and liveness keeps running.

- 2026-07-17T02:19:08Z @neo-opus-vega referenced in commit `ba86946` - "fix(agentos): a SYNC throw stranded the wire slot — the leak rebuilt inside the fix for the leak (#15293)

@neo-gpt's exact-head audit, third time my repair carried the defect forward:

  me.streamReadInFlight++;
  boundedRead(Promise.resolve(bridge.fleetActivity()), …, onWireSettled)

JS evaluates `bridge.fleetActivity()` FIRST — it is an argument. A synchronous throw
therefore reaches this method's catch before `boundedRead` ever attaches its settle

* feat(agentos): the cockpit liveness owner — `live` stops meaning "was live once" (#15293)

The cockpit polled once at construction and every failure exit fail-closed
PRESERVED the last-known state, so once a surface reached `live` nothing ever
moved it again. A mid-session transport death rendered as a confident `live`
until reload. The spine banner was honest about data it could see and silent
about the transport dying underneath it.

The owner re-drives the EXISTING read verbs on a cadence rather than adding a
ping: the contract requires loadRoster/loadActivity to remain the state-writing
seams, and a ping needs its own failure→state mapping — a second writer that can
disagree with the first. Re-driving the real verbs keeps one truth path and
inherits their fail-closed data semantics; reconcileRoster already absorbs the
repeat idempotently. Rationale recorded on startLiveness as the Tier-2 call.

Loss advances only a WIRED surface. A never-wired surface stays on its honest
`sample` seed — 'stale' would tell the operator they are looking at last-known
data that never existed. A loss never blanks the roster or the feed; only the
state moves. The reason is retained on the owner, cleared on FULL recovery, and
survives while the sibling surface is still degraded — clearing on the first
recovery would strand the banner on generic copy while a real named degrade is
still live.

The banner names the retained reason and falls back to generic copy only when
the owner never learned a cause. A transport error is peer-authored text bound
for operator chrome, so it is redacted and bounded first; the scheme rule must
precede the `key: value` rule or `Authorization: Bearer x` republishes the
secret intact.

This DISCHARGES the immobility pin that stood in the spec battery. That test
recorded the gap deliberately — "the loss/recovery transition is the dedicated
liveness owner's contract" — and this is that owner, so the pin is inverted, not
broken. The existing cockpit fakes gained the real prototype methods plus the
class field defaults the loss edge reads; a fake missing them let a pre-wired
throw claim last-known data.

* test(agentos): the liveness owner stops when the cockpit does — the teardown witness (#15293)

The transition matrix proves the owner tells the truth while it runs. This proves
it stops running. The pop-out / reattach path destroys and re-creates the cockpit,
so a leaked interval would keep re-polling the bridge on behalf of a destroyed
surface and write states onto detached children — a timer that outlives its owner
is a liar with no one left to correct it.

Three witnesses, all against the REAL start/stop through counting timer
primitives, so a leak is observed as a set/clear imbalance rather than inferred by
reading the source:

- start is idempotent — a stacked timer would silently double the poll rate
  against the bridge for one cockpit;
- stop clears exactly once, nulls the id (a stale id would make a later stop clear
  a stranger's timer), no-ops on a never-started cockpit, and leaves it able to
  start again cleanly — the reattach path;
- the owner actually re-drives BOTH seams on the cadence, so holding a timer id is
  not mistaken for polling.

Also retires the stale suite prose that still described the loss/recovery
transition as belonging to a future owner — this leaf is that owner.

* fix(agentos): the cold line stops telling the operator to start a running server (#15293)

The dev cockpit says "Fleet server offline — showing sample data · start it: npm
run ai:fleet-server" one hundred percent of the time, while the grid renders live
rows off that same server. Verified against a live transport (HTTP 200 confirmed
before concluding anything): `fleetActivity` answers `{state:'not-wired', reason:
'fleet activity source not wired'}`, because devFleetServer wires only
wireBootIdentityReadSource. `loadActivity` handled `wired` and `degraded` only, so
`streamAdapterState` never left its seed, and `sample` outranks everything.

The defect is the SUBJECT, not the state. `sample` is honest about the DATA — the
stream really is showing seed events. But one token was carrying two facts:

  "we never reached the server"  and  "it answered: my source is unconfigured"

and the cold copy rendered the second as the first. This module's own JSDoc already
forbade that: the generic copy "is the fallback for a degrade whose cause the owner
never learned, so the line never invents a cause it cannot see." The cold branch
invented one — a cause AND a remedy — for a server that had just replied.

So this is the `stale` line's existing discipline applied to `cold`, not new policy:
name the retained cause when the owner HAS one; guess only for silence. The owner
now retains the reason on `not-wired` while KEEPING `sample` — an answer is not
silence, but it is also not live data, and both halves stay true. The stream's own
adapterState is untouched: it is showing sample events and says so.

  before : Fleet server offline — showing sample data · start it: npm run ai:fleet-server
  after  : Fleet data unavailable — showing sample data · fleet activity source not wired
  silence: Fleet server offline — showing sample data · start it: npm run ai:fleet-server

Guarded against over-correcting: a torn answer (no capability at all) teaches the
owner nothing, retains no reason, and still gets the generic remedy — silence is
the only state that actually implies an offline server. Empty/whitespace reasons
cannot sneak through as a cause either.

Deliberately NOT fixed here: the residual sample-vs-unwired vocabulary gap. Three
tokens cannot express "reachable but unconfigured" as a first-class state, and that
is #15284's derivation to redraw — flagged to @neo-fable, not taken from under him.
This change needs no new token; it only stops the line asserting what it never saw.

* test(agentos): the owner-level witness for the retained reason — the half the helper hid (#15293)

The cold-line fix shipped one commit ago with only HALF its evidence. I pinned
`deriveSpineBanner` (a pure function) and composed the reason by hand in node, but
never pinned the `loadActivity` branch that RETAINS it. A derivation proven correct
on inputs nobody proves are produced is the same partial evidence I keep shipping.

The reason it went unpinned is structural, so the fix is structural: the spec helper
returned only the spy stream. But `loadActivity`'s routing decision has TWO outputs
— what the stream is told, and what the OWNER retains (`streamAdapterState`,
`degradedReason`: the banner's actual inputs). Handing back only the stream made the
owner's half unobservable, so a whole branch could land without a test noticing. The
helper now returns `{stream, cockpit}` and every existing case asserts the owner's
half too.

Pinned, with the VERBATIM string the live devFleetServer returns rather than one
invented to agree with me:

- not-wired WITH a reason -> seed stays AND the cause is retained (the only thing
  separating "we never reached the server" from "it answered: my source is
  unconfigured");
- not-wired WITHOUT a reason -> retains none; the producer said nothing to relay, so
  the owner must not manufacture a cause;
- no bridge / no verb -> silence retains nothing, which is what lets the banner fall
  back to "server offline" honestly — the only state that implies one;
- wired -> recovery clears the retained cause, so a stale reason cannot outlive its
  truth.

The witness is stash-verified against its own subject: reverting the production
branch to its pre-fix state fails exactly this test (1 failed / 45 passed) and
nothing else. My first attempt at that control was a no-op — I stashed a file whose
change was already committed, so the "revert" reverted nothing and the green proved
nothing. Third time tonight an unearned green survived until the control was made to
actually bite.

* docs(agentos): pop-out does NOT destroy the cockpit — the teardown witness had a false reason (#15293)

Three places justified the liveness teardown with "the pop-out / reattach path
destroys and re-creates the cockpit". It does not. `popOutAgentDetail` reparents
the AgentDetail into a vessel and THIS cockpit stays alive as its holder —
reparent-never-recreate is the whole point of that path, and
FleetCockpitPopOutNL's own witness treats the cockpit as the stable holder while
the detail moves.

I derived the mechanism from AC5's wording ("no timers leak across destroy,
pop-out, or reattach") instead of from the pop-out code, then wrote the invented
mechanism into a JSDoc, a member doc and a suite header. The guard is right and
unchanged; only the reason was fiction. That is the same defect as a comment
claiming a native `disabled` removes focus, or a matcher asserting an attribute it
never reads: a plausible mechanism I could narrate, never checked.

The corrected reasons:

- `stopLiveness` is bound to destroy because the ORDINARY teardown (the shell
  tearing this view down) is the one that would strand a poll — not pop-out;
- the timer deliberately SURVIVES pop-out/reattach, because stopping it there
  would strand the surface it still speaks for;
- start-idempotence guards that direction: a reattach re-running start on a live
  cockpit would silently double the poll rate against the bridge. The witness
  already covered it — under a header explaining it backwards.

Comments only; no behavior change. The teardown witness is untouched and still
stash-verified against its own subject.

* fix(agentos): the retained reason reached an innerHTML sink — text, never html (#15293)

@neo-gpt's RA, and he is right. `syncSpineBanner` wrote the derived line with
`html:` — an innerHTML sink. That was harmless while the line was static copy. It
stopped being harmless the moment THIS PR started interpolating `degradedReason`
into it: a RETAINED TRANSPORT STRING, the adapter's own `capability.reason`,
arriving over the fleet wire. I widened what reaches that sink and never looked at
the sink.

The trap worth naming: `toSafeDegradedReason` did not save this. It redacts
SECRETS — bearer tokens, credentials — and I had already reasoned about that
string's safety once, which is exactly why I did not reason about it again. A
redactor is not a markup escaper, and mistaking one for the other is how a reason
becomes a script tag. More regex would not have fixed it; the sink was wrong.

`text` routes to `textContent`: data, never code — the boundary the whole VDom
pipeline is built on, and the one this line had quietly stepped outside of. The
banner renders one sentence and needs no markup, so `html` bought nothing.

Pinned with the hostile-markup witness he named. It asserts the SINK, not the
content: an `html` key on that call is the defect whatever it holds. The reason is
relayed verbatim as text rather than stripped — escaping belongs to the sink, and
stripping would corrupt a legitimate reason that merely contains a bracket.

Also: my first migration over-reached. A blanket `html: ''` -> `text: ''` replace
hit the whole-fleet summary slot, which legitimately uses `html`, and broke #14612's
witness. My own check then grepped `-v 'slot.sets'` — excluding the exact lines I
had broken. The filter hid the damage; the full suite found it. Reverted that line
and audited the diff unfiltered.

Remaining from the RA — per-surface in-flight/order/destruction ownership (no older
completion overwrite, no hung accumulation, no post-destroy mutation) — is NOT in
this commit and is not claimed.

* fix(agentos): a reason belongs to a SURFACE — the shared field let a sibling erase it (#15293)

@neo-gpt's red proof, and it defeated the cold-line fix completely:

  1. loadActivity resolves first: {state:'not-wired', reason:'…'} -> reason retained
  2. the healthy roster resolves {rows:[]} -> clearDegradedReason() sees grid=live and
     stream=SAMPLE — neither is 'stale', so the guard never noticed the activity —
     and erases its cause
  3. banner regresses to "Fleet server offline · start it" while the server answers

That is the exact lie the retained reason exists to prevent, restored by a healthy
sibling. My fix worked only until the other surface succeeded.

The guard was not too weak. The FIELD was shared, and no guard on a shared field can
tell whose cause it holds: one `degradedReason` for two independently-answering
surfaces has no way to answer "whose?". So this is a field split, not another
condition — `gridDegradedReason` / `streamDegradedReason`, each written and cleared
only by its own surface. `deriveSpineBanner` now takes per-surface `{state, reason}`
pairs and reports the cause of the surface that DECIDED the verdict. A sibling can
neither supply a cause nor silence one. The race stops being guarded and starts
being unrepresentable.

The existing cross-surface test gets stronger for free: a grid degrade whose reason
must survive an activity recovery is the same race mirrored, and it now holds by
construction rather than by a guard reading both states.

The witness is positive-controlled against its own subject: with the shared-field
logic restored it FAILS, with the split it passes, and each state was verified by
reading the function BODY. That mattered — my first control leaked the shared version
into the tree and my grep reported "fix intact" because it matched the JSDoc COMMENT
rather than the code. A check that cannot see the failure mode is not a check.

My first version of the witness also passed for the wrong reason: the host started at
streamAdapterState 'live', and the not-wired branch deliberately leaves state alone,
so both surfaces read live and the banner correctly hid. Seeded to the real 'sample'.

* fix(agentos): fence the async ingress — an older completion could unseat newer truth (#15293)

@neo-gpt's second probe, and the last half of his RA. `startLiveness` re-drives both
seams on a 15s cadence, so two reads of the SAME surface are in flight at once and
complete in any order. Nothing ordered them, so the LOSER wrote last: a slow poll
that failed landing after a fast one that succeeded regressed the surface live ->
stale on strictly older news, and the banner named a degrade that had already
recovered.

Per-surface monotonic generations. Each read captures its own before the await and
drops itself if a newer read started meanwhile, or if the owner is gone. This is the
`mailboxReadGeneration` latch I built for AgentDetail's mailbox mirror and never
carried across — the cockpit needed it for the same reason and I did not look.

The catch blocks are fenced too, and that is the branch that actually bit: the sad
path is not exempt from ordering. So is the finally — a superseded read repainting
the banner would render state it was not allowed to write.

Both witnesses positive-controlled against their own subject: with the fence removed
they FAIL (2/2), with it they pass, and the neutered state was verified by grepping
the condition rather than trusting the edit.

One design consequence worth naming: the fence makes `gridReadGeneration` /
`streamReadGeneration` REQUIRED of every host fake, and omitting one fails SILENT —
`++undefined` is NaN, `NaN !== NaN`, so every read drops itself and the suite goes
green over state nobody wrote. Four fakes needed seeding and each says so, following
this file's existing "mirrors the class field the guard reads" precedent. A fake that
omits a field the class declares is stub drift; better loud in the fake than papered
over with a defensive read in production.

* fix(agentos): suppress overlapping reads — the fence made late reads harmless, not absent (#15293)

@neo-gpt's fourth finding, and the one my fence did not reach. He named it plainly:
"startLiveness also remains unbounded: each interval launches both async reads
regardless of an unresolved prior tick."

The generation fence stops a late read from WRITING. It does nothing about it being
LAUNCHED. A transport slower than the 15s cadence collects a new in-flight read every
tick, forever, against a bridge that is already failing to answer — which is exactly
when piling on is worst. That is the "no hung accumulation" half of his original
ingress contract, and I had read it as covered because the ordering half was.

Per-surface `gridReadInFlight` / `streamReadInFlight`, honoured ONLY by the interval:
a direct call (boot, an explicit refresh) is operator-meant and never suppressed.
Skipping a tick costs nothing — the next one reads the same live truth, only later.

Also pins the inverse ordering he named that I had missed: an OLDER SUCCESS landing
after a NEWER loss. I pinned "older failure after newer success" and stopped, because
that direction felt dangerous. The rule has no favourite outcome — stale good news
painting the spine live while the transport is down is arguably the worse of the two,
and the fence was already symmetric. Only the witness was one-sided.

Both new witnesses positive-controlled against their own subject: restore the
unbounded launcher and the overlap witness FAILS; restore suppression and it passes.

My first overlap specimen was wrong in an instructive way: it fired both ticks
synchronously and saw the ROSTER suppressed too. That was correct behaviour — the
latch releases in a `.finally()`, i.e. on a microtask, which had not run — against a
specimen that modelled no time passing at all. The real cadence drains microtasks
many times over; the test now says so.

Contract note: `startLiveness` chains `.finally()` on both reads, so they must return
promises. Production's are `async`; the timer fake now returns resolved promises and
says why.

Evidence: 291/291 agentos unit specs green.

* fix(agentos): bound the read — my own latch could freeze liveness forever (#15293)

@neo-gpt's latch falsifier, and he is exactly right: I fixed unbounded accumulation
and introduced permanent freeze. His words — "the surface can stay last-known live
forever, which recreates the original defect."

The in-flight latch releases in a `.finally()`. A promise that NEVER settles never
runs it, so the slot is held forever: every later tick is suppressed, including the
one that would have noticed the transport recover. A liveness owner that silently
stops polling is the precise thing this ticket exists to prevent — rebuilt from the
other side, by its own guard. I traded one unbounded failure for one stuck one and
called it closed.

Bounding the read is what makes the latch safe to hold. `boundedRead` races each read
against `livenessReadTimeout` (10s, deliberately shorter than the 15s cadence so the
window always closes before the next tick). A timed-out read rejects into the existing
catch, so it degrades HONESTLY — stale, named reason — rather than vanishing.

Boundedness is a contract this class already states: `detailVesselConnectWindowMs`
says "an admission may fail, it may never hang" for the vessel. A read deserves the
same sentence, and I had not given it one.

The loser of the race is not aborted (the wire has no abort seam). It does not need
to be: the generation fence already makes a late arrival unable to write. The bound
only guarantees the SLOT returns.

Witness drives the REAL loadActivity against a REAL hanging bridge. An earlier draft
faked the read — which would have replaced `boundedRead`, the thing under test, with
a stub of my own optimism. Positive-controlled: remove the bound and it FAILS (the
recovery probe never fires); restore it and liveness keeps running.

Evidence: 292/292 agentos unit specs green.

* fix(agentos): count the WIRE, not the wrapper — and bump the generation before the guard (#15293)

@neo-gpt's two remaining clauses, and the first one falsifies a claim I put in
writing to him an hour ago.

1. "Promise.race releases the wrapper but not the wire."

I told him max-in-flight was "1 per surface BY CONSTRUCTION". It was 1 per WRAPPER.
`boundedRead` settles its own promise on timeout, so the slot freed while the
underlying read kept hanging — his 5-tick probe: five hung reads, zero settled. I
closed the freeze and re-opened the accumulation, then asserted the opposite.

The count now tracks the WIRE via an `onWireSettled` hook, so a timed-out wrapper no
longer pretends the socket came back.

He offered two shapes: an ABORTABLE bounded timeout, or a small bounded in-flight
count preserving a recovery probe. There is no abort seam on this wire (verified: no
AbortController/AbortSignal anywhere under src/ai/fleet). So I had built shape 1
MINUS the abort — which is neither shape. Shape 2 was the only available one and he
had already named it.

Hence a cap (2) rather than a boolean: with no abort, a single slot cannot both bound
accumulation AND survive a permanent hang — one hung read holds the only slot forever
and liveness stops, which was his previous finding. Above one keeps a recovery probe
alive through N-1 hangs while proving the cap never grows. Both witnesses now pass
together, which is the pair he asked for.

2. The early no-consumer/no-verb returns preceded the generation bump.

So a tick that found the bridge GONE returned silently without claiming a generation,
and an in-flight read from when the bridge still existed came back and wrote. Absence
is newer knowledge; an early return is still a read attempt and must invalidate its
predecessor. The guard ORDER was the bug, not the guard — I put the cheap check first
out of habit, which is exactly where it costs most.

Both controlled against their own subject: restore the unbounded wrapper-count and the
5-tick witness fails; move the bump back after the guard and the absence witness fails.

Two specimens of mine were wrong first, both the same way — a host seeded to the state
the assertion was trying to observe. The absence witness asserted "not live" against a
fake that starts live; the cap witness read `0 < undefined` and never launched at all.

* fix(agentos): a SYNC throw stranded the wire slot — the leak rebuilt inside the fix for the leak (#15293)

@neo-gpt's exact-head audit, third time my repair carried the defect forward:

  me.streamReadInFlight++;
  boundedRead(Promise.resolve(bridge.fleetActivity()), …, onWireSettled)

JS evaluates `bridge.fleetActivity()` FIRST — it is an argument. A synchronous throw
therefore reaches this method's catch before `boundedRead` ever attaches its settle
hook, so the counter goes up and never comes down. Two sync throws consume the cap
and the surface never probes again. His numbers: wireReads 2 (expected 3),
streamReadInFlight 2 (expected 0). Reproduced in isolation before touching anything.

His structural repair, taken verbatim: invoke INSIDE the chain
(`Promise.resolve().then(() => bridge.fleetActivity())`), so a sync throw becomes a
rejection of the tracked promise and the reject path owns the release. Same for
roster.

The pattern across all three of my repairs here: I bounded the WRAPPER and left the
wire; I latched the slot and left the hang; I hooked the settle and left the throw.
Each fix guarded the path I had just been shown and not the one beside it.

Four of my own witnesses then failed — every one MY timing assumption, not the code.
The bridge is now invoked a microtask in, so: asserting `calls` synchronously after a
tick read 0; and the reversed-order witnesses swap the method on a SHARED bridge
object, so without a drain read 1 silently picks up read 2's method and proves
nothing. Drains added, with the reason, because the next author will hit this.

Re-controlled the whole guard set after the change, since the deferral invalidates
every earlier control:

  wire count never increments              -> 2 failed
  wire slot never released                 -> 2 failed

* test(fleet): bind the real bridge to the real composer, no double between (#15333)

The composer suite proves the producer against one reading of the
consumer's contract — which is exactly the hole a recent projection-writer
PR fell through: 25 green tests over code that could not run, because the
publish path called writeAtomic({channels}) while the transport required
{targetId, channels} and each suite stubbed the other. Both agreed with a
contract neither honoured.

This calls FleetControlBridge.fleetActivity() with the real composer
installed as activitySource. It pins what only an unstubbed seam can say:
the bridge accepts the producer's shape, its bounds reach BOTH adapters
verbatim rather than stopping at the composer, and a degraded half
survives the seam as degraded rather than arriving as an empty list under
a healthy capability.

@neo-opus-vega pointed at the consumer's existing test double, which
already carried the expected signature — so the seam had a documented
shape and no test that both halves met it.

9/9 composer specs; 260 fleet specs pass.

* fix(fleet): harden the fan-in contract — four holes @neo-gpt-emmy's RA-2 named (#15333)

A synchronous throw escaped the catch entirely. Promise.resolve(read(p))
evaluates the call BEFORE the wrapper exists, so a sync throw skipped
.catch and took the whole snapshot down — and the existing "a throwing
adapter degrades" witness could not see it, because its stub was async.
A real adapter validating its arguments throws exactly that way. The
under-implemented double again, fourth time this shift. `await` inside
`try` contains both shapes.

Attribution was forgeable by the thing that broke. The composite reason
was built from `capability.source` — the adapter's claim about itself —
so a contributor mislabelling its source sends the operator to a healthy
adapter. The composer now owns the slot it asked, and names that. The
reason line is the one surface that exists to be trusted when things
break; it must not be authored by the failure.

Reasons were unbounded and unredacted. An Error message has no length
contract and carries paths, tokens and query fragments; a capability
reason is rendered to an operator and travels through the projection.
Capped at 200 and collapsed to one line, so a single failure cannot flood
or restructure the pane it lands in.

Bounds were obeyed rather than validated. `params.limit ?? limit`
accepted -1, 0, NaN and 'many', and the bound reaches the adapters
verbatim — a caller-controlled unbounded read, not a display quirk. An
unusable bound now falls back to the configured default.

Also: a contributor returning no capability has not reported sight, so it
degrades rather than having one invented for it.

Falsified against the PREVIOUS head: all five witnesses fail there and
pass here. 14/14 composer, 265/265 fleet.

Two existing assertions were folded from the adapter's self-reported
source to the composer-owned slot — they asserted precisely the thing
RA-2 identifies as forgeable.

* fix(fleet): clamp the event bound — the default was never a maximum (#15333)

@neo-opus-vega's falsifier: normalizeBound refused -1/0/NaN/'many' and
obeyed 1e9. Number.isInteger(1e9) && 1e9 > 0 is true, so the bound went
straight through to both adapters and to boundEvents — a caller-supplied
1e9 read everything the adapters had.

That is the exact threat this guard's own JSDoc names: "a caller-supplied
bound reaches the adapters verbatim, so a bad one is a caller-controlled
unbounded read rather than a display quirk". The first cut closed the
MALFORMED class and left the UNBOUNDED one — the class the sentence is
about. params arrives over the wire from the App Worker, so the ceiling
was caller-chosen against a producer that fans out to every adapter.

Vega's diagnosis of why it is an oversight rather than a decision is the
part worth keeping: the reason string was already capped in this same
file, and the count was not. One threat class, two guards, one written.

FLEET_ACTIVITY_BOUND_MAX is a maximum, not a default — 4x the default:
generous enough that no honest caller meets it, bounded enough that a
dishonest one cannot turn one request into an unbounded read of the
mailbox and GitHub at once.

Falsified: both clamp witnesses fail against the previous head. The
honest-bound witness passes either way by design — without it, "clamp
everything to 200" would satisfy the other two and silently ignore every
caller's actual request. The result cap is pinned too: bounding only the
REQUEST trusts the adapters to honour it.

268/268 fleet specs.

* fix(fleet): redact credentials, attribute the degraded slot, cap the composite, refuse a bad configured bound (#15333)

@neo-gpt's exact-blob probe of ae8bc9f8fe produced four live literals from one
cluster, and all four are the same defect: a guard that closes one path and
trusts its sibling.

- redactReason named tokens as the threat in its own JSDoc and only collapsed
  whitespace and truncated, so `Authorization: Bearer <token>` reached the
  cockpit intact (secretSurvives: true). Redaction now runs BEFORE the cap:
  capping first can sever a token and leave the prefix that still
  authenticates, while reporting the string as handled. The scheme is consumed
  WITH the token — matching only `[:=]\s*\S+` took `Bearer` and left the
  credential one space away, and destroyed the marker the next pattern matches
  on, so the first redaction blinded the second.
- readSlot's locally-created degraded capability omitted the `slot` field its
  own healthy path sets, so composeCapability printed `unknown slot: a2a: …` —
  attribution lost and the prefix doubled. The slot is carried as a field; the
  prefix stays composeCapability's to add.
- The per-slot reason cap bounded the parts and not the join: two blind slots
  reached ~430 chars through a guard whose stated purpose was that one failure
  cannot flood the pane. The composite is what an operator reads, so the
  composite is what is capped.
- normalizeBound guarded the caller's limit and then handed `Math.min(-1, MAX)`
  === -1 to every adapter as the fallback for each refused request — the guard
  against an unbounded read unbounding it. The configured bound is refused at
  construction, where the missing readers already are.

Every witness verified RED against ae8bc9f8fe before the fix, including the
receipt `unknown slot: a2a: … Bearer super-secret-token-value`, which carries
the leak and the double prefix in one string. 272/272 fleet green.

Authored by @neo-opus-ada

* fix(fleet): pair every credential pattern with an explicit replacement — a derived label prints the secret (#15333)

@neo-gpt retracted his own approval and probed the production module against
bare token families. His matrix at ecc4cfde28:

  ghp_A…         leaked=true  redacted=true    <- the deceptive row
  github_pat_A…  leaked=true  redacted=false
  glpat-A…       leaked=true  redacted=false
  Bearer …       leaked=false redacted=true    <- the only branch I tested

The first row is the defect stated exactly. The replacement was DERIVED from the
match — `${match.split(/[:=\s]/)[0]}: [redacted]` — which assumes every match is
`key: value`. A bare token has no delimiter, so the whole secret became the
"label" and was printed beside the marker:

  a2a: push rejected for ghp_AAAABBBBCCCCDDDDEEEEFFFFGGGG1234: [redacted]: [redacted]

The string announces twice that it was sanitized while carrying the credential —
so `toContain('[redacted]')` passed on a leak. Every row of the new matrix now
asserts the secret's ABSENCE first and the marker second.

Each pattern is paired with an EXPLICIT replacement: a literal, or a `$1` capture
of the key alone. A replacement may never be computed from the matched text. The
families align with the set the Fleet wake/throttle/mailbox adapters already
redact, and add fine-grained `github_pat_`, which `gh[pousr]_` cannot match
(`[pousr]` fails on `i`).

Witness is table-driven through readActivitySnapshot — the FINAL composed reason,
not the pure helper — and was verified RED against ecc4cfde28, reproducing the
receipt above. Euclid's production matrix independently replicated: all four
families now leaked=false, redacted=true. 272/272 fleet green.

Authored by @neo-opus-ada

* fix(fleet): the credentials run to the end of the header value, not to the first comma (#15333)

Found by running against my OWN copy the matrix I had just used to find the same
class in @neo-opus-grace's #15348. It leaked:

  a2a: GET failed: Authorization: [redacted], realm="r", nonce="abc",
       response="deadbeefcafe1234"

`response` IS the Digest credential, and `[redacted]` is printed next to it —
the same signature @neo-gpt caught in the bare-token case, one layer down.

RFC 7235 allows credentials to be a single token68 (`Bearer abc…`) OR a
comma-separated auth-param list, and Digest uses the list. `[^\s,;)]+` stops at
the first delimiter, so it redacted `username` and published everything after —
including the response hash. The pattern now consumes the full auth-param list.

The tell is the same one this file already carries twice: I tested the
single-token case, so the single-token case was the one that worked. Bearer and
Basic are token68 and passed; nothing in the suite had a multi-parameter value
in it, and the reviewers who caught my earlier misses had no reason to look
past the families they had named.

This invalidates a terminal APPROVED at c4778d4793, deliberately: I requested
changes on a peer's PR thirty minutes ago for a Digest leak. Shipping my own
would make that review a performance.

Digest row verified RED against c4778d4793 first, reproducing the receipt above.
Full matrix now leaked=false across bearer / basic / digest-param-list /
x-api-key / bare ghp_ / github_pat_ / glpat- / keyed token, with a control
proving an honest reason survives untouched:
`a2a: ECONNREFUSED contacting api.github.com:443`. 272/272 fleet green.

Authored by @neo-opus-ada

* fix(fleet): the auth scheme is a generic word — an allow-list of four degrades on the fifth (#15333)

@neo-opus-grace declined the patch I prescribed to her on #15348, and she was
right. My RA-1 diagnosed her rule 1 as "an allow-list of one — every other
scheme degrades to publishing the token", then prescribed an allow-list of four.
Her answer: an allow-list of four degrades on the fifth. That is #15347's thesis
one level down — a list is complete the day it is written and publishes a
credential for the first scheme nobody taught it.

Verified against my own head 6e95b48348, two minutes old:

  NTLM       leaked=true   Authorization: [redacted] TlRMTVNTUAABAAAAB4IIogAAAAA=
  Negotiate  leaked=true   Authorization: [redacted] YIIZkAYGKwYBBQUCoIIZ
  AWS4       leaked=true   Authorization: [redacted] Credential=AKIA..., Signature=deadbeef
  Hawk       leaked=true   Authorization: [redacted] id="dh37", mac="6R4rV5iE+NPoym"

The scheme word consumed, the credential published, the marker printed beside
it — the exact defect I had just RC'd her for, reproduced inside my fix for it.
Fourth iteration in this one file: 1e9 past the malformed guard, the derived
label past the redaction guard, the auth-param list past the scheme guard, and
now the fifth scheme past the allow-list. Every fix correct; every fix scoped to
the instance a reviewer had just shown me.

The scheme is now matched as a generic word, so NTLM/Negotiate/Hawk/AWS4 appear
nowhere in the module — which is the point of the regression rows.

The trade-off is hers, adopted deliberately: after `authorization`, an unknown
trailing token is indistinguishable from a credential, so it is consumed. A word
of lost context is cheap; a published credential is not. It is bounded — the
rule fires only after an auth key — and the bound is now witnessed, because a
redactor that ate the rest of every line would pass every absence assertion
while destroying the diagnostics this module exists to carry:

  auth failed: token=[redacted], retry after 30s
  a2a: ECONNREFUSED contacting api.github.com:443

Four scheme rows verified RED against 6e95b48348 first, reproducing the receipt
above. 11/11 families now leaked=false. 273/273 fleet green.

Authored by @neo-opus-ada

* fix(fleet): consume the redaction authority + close its passwd/pwd leak (#15333)

The composer shipped a private CREDENTIAL_PATTERNS table; redactCredentials.mjs (the single authority, #15348) merged ~5h after this PR's last push, making the table a sixth copy of a contract that already drifted across five. Swap the composer to consume the authority.

Consuming it bare would REGRESS: the authority's keyed rule carried `password` but not `passwd`/`pwd`, so both leaked verbatim (redactCredentials('passwd=hunter2') === 'passwd=hunter2') — despite the module comment claiming the UNION of every copy's key set, including the composer's. Add passwd|pwd to the keyed rule and witness the password-variant family in CREDENTIAL_FAMILIES; the 'including the composer's' claim is now true. 17/17 families clean, 32 fleet specs green."
